cse-2021-2-cs-13.approach: An intermediate representation (IR) is a form that *encodes the program itself* between source and target. Three-address code, ASTs and CFGs all do; the symbol table only stores attributes of names and cannot reproduce the program.

steps.title: What counts as an IR
steps.body: An IR must represent the **computation** of the source program so later phases can analyse and translate it. Common IRs: linear (three-address code, quadruples), tree-shaped (syntax tree / AST, DAG) and graph-shaped (control flow graph of basic blocks).

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body:
- Three address code: linear IR, e.g. `t1 = b * c`.
- AST: hierarchical IR produced by the parser.
- CFG: graph IR whose nodes are basic blocks of three-address code.
- Symbol table: a lookup structure (name → type, scope, offset) shared by all phases; it holds **no statements or control flow**, so it is not a representation of the program.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only the **symbol table** is not an intermediate representation → option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Three-address code is the classic linear IR used for optimisation and code generation.
The AST is a tree IR built by the parser and used for semantic analysis and translation.
The CFG (basic blocks + jump edges) is a graph IR used by data-flow analysis and optimisation.
Correct: the symbol table only records information about identifiers; it does not encode the program’s operations, so it is not an IR.

pitfalls: Thinking “anything the compiler builds” is an IR — the symbol table is an auxiliary data structure.
cse-2021-2-cs-13.verification: You can regenerate code from 3AC, an AST or a CFG of 3AC blocks, but not from a symbol table alone.

cse-2021-2-cs-14.approach: Check each statement against the definitions: turnaround = completion − arrival (contains waiting), scheduling goals, what RR needs to know, and how preemption is triggered.

steps.title: (A) Turnaround time
steps.body: $\text{TAT} = \text{completion} - \text{arrival} = \text{waiting} + \text{burst} (+\text{I/O})$. So turnaround time **includes** waiting time — **true**.

steps.title: (B) Scheduling goal
steps.body: Goals are to maximise CPU utilisation **and throughput**, and minimise turnaround, waiting and response time. “Only maximise utilisation and minimise throughput” is wrong on both counts — **false**.

steps.title: (C) Round robin
steps.body: RR just gives each ready process a fixed time quantum in FIFO order; it never needs the burst length (unlike SJF/SRTF) — **true**.

steps.title: (D) Preemption
steps.body: To take the CPU away from a running process the OS must regain control, which needs a **hardware timer interrupt** (and mode switching support) — **true**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: turnaround time = waiting time + execution (+ I/O) time.
Throughput must be maximised, not minimised, and utilisation is not the only goal.
Correct: RR is time-slice based and needs no prior knowledge of burst times.
Correct: preemption relies on a hardware timer interrupt to return control to the scheduler.

pitfalls: Confusing RR with SJF/SRTF, which do need burst-time estimates.
cse-2021-2-cs-14.verification: Each statement checked directly against the textbook definitions of the scheduling criteria and mechanisms.

cse-2021-2-cs-16.approach: Label the 7-node complete tree 1–7 level by level. BFS takes the root and its two children; DFS takes the root, one child and that child’s child. They differ in exactly one element.

steps.title: Label the tree
steps.body: A complete binary tree with 7 nodes is perfect: root 1, children 2, 3, and leaves 4, 5, 6, 7.

steps.title: BFS
steps.body: Level order visits $1, 2, 3, \dots$ so $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$.

steps.title: DFS
steps.body: DFS goes deep first: $1, 2, 4, \dots$ (or $1,3,6$ / $1,3,7$ / $1,2,5$ for other child orders), so $B = \{1, 2, 4\}$.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: $A - B = \{3\}$, so $|A - B| = 1$. Whatever child order DFS uses, $B$ = root + one child + one grandchild, so $A-B$ is always the other child: **1**.

pitfalls: Computing $|A \cup B|$ or $|A \cap B|$ instead of the set difference.
cse-2021-2-cs-16.verification: For every DFS order, A ∩ B = {root, one child}, leaving exactly one element in A − B.

cse-2021-2-cs-17.approach: Every state has a transition on both symbols and every path of 3 symbols reaches the accepting state, which loops on 0,1. So the DFA accepts exactly the strings of length ≥ 3; all $2^8$ strings of length 8 qualify.

steps.title: After 1 symbol
steps.body: From the start state $q_0$: on 0 → $q_1$, on 1 → $q_2$. Either way we are in $\{q_1, q_2\}$, not accepting.

steps.title: After 2 symbols
steps.body: $q_1$ and $q_2$ both go on 0 → $q_3$ and on 1 → $q_4$. Every length-2 string ends in $\{q_3, q_4\}$, not accepting.

steps.title: After 3+ symbols
steps.body: $q_3, q_4$ go on 0,1 to the accepting $q_5$, which loops on 0,1. Hence $L = \{w : |w| \ge 3\}$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Every string of length 8 is accepted: $2^8 = $ **256**.

pitfalls: Assuming only some branches lead to acceptance — check that the crossing edges make every path reach the final state.
cse-2021-2-cs-17.verification: Length-8 strings: the DFA is in q5 after the 3rd symbol for any prefix, and stays there; so all 256 are accepted.

cse-2021-2-cs-18.approach: Convert the binary fraction using place values $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, \dots$ and read off the digits.

cse-2021-2-cs-19.approach: Split the 32-bit address into tag | set index | offset. Offset and tag widths are known, so the index width gives the number of sets, and lines ÷ sets is the associativity.

steps.title: Offset and lines
steps.body: Block = 64 B $= 2^6$ → offset = 6 bits. Lines $= \dfrac{2^{11}}{2^6} = 2^5 = 32$.

steps.title: Associativity
steps.body: $\dfrac{32 \text{ lines}}{16 \text{ sets}} = $ **2-way**.

cse-2021-2-cs-19.verification: Check: 2 ways × 16 sets × 64 B = 2048 B = 2 KB.

cse-2021-2-cs-20.approach: Cycles stolen per second × bits per stolen cycle gives the device rate.

steps.title: Cycles used for DMA
steps.body: $2\times10^6 \text{ cycles/s} \times 0.005 = 10^4$ cycles/s.

steps.title: Rate
steps.body: Each stolen cycle moves 8 bits: $10^4 \times 8 = $ **80000 bits/s**.

cse-2021-2-cs-21.approach: The file is not sorted on ANum, so the index on ANum is a dense (secondary) index: one entry per record. Use an unspanned blocking factor.

steps.title: Blocking factor
steps.body: $\left\lfloor \dfrac{4096}{19} \right\rfloor = 215$ (since $215 \times 19 = 4085 \le 4096 < 4104 = 216\times 19$).

steps.title: Blocks
steps.body: Entries = 150000 (dense). $\left\lceil \dfrac{150000}{215} \right\rceil = \lceil 697.67 \rceil = $ **698**.

pitfalls: Treating it as a sparse index (one entry per data block) — that only works on the ordering key RollNo.

cse-2021-2-cs-23.approach: The function is the subtraction form of Euclid’s algorithm (returning 1 early if either argument hits 1), so it returns gcd(15, 255).

steps.title: Recognise the pattern
steps.body: Replacing the larger argument by the difference keeps the gcd unchanged; it stops when $x = y$ (the gcd) or when one becomes 1 (gcd 1).

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: $y > x$ each time: $(15,255) \to (15,240) \to (15,225) \to \dots \to (15,30) \to (15,15)$, i.e. 16 subtractions of 15 until $y = 15$. Then $x == y$ returns **15**.

cse-2021-2-cs-24.approach: The null space is spanned by one non-zero vector, so nullity = 1; apply rank–nullity with 5 columns.

steps.title: Nullity
steps.body: All solutions of $P\mathbf{x}=0$ are multiples of one non-zero vector → $\dim N(P) = 1$.

steps.title: Rank–nullity
steps.body: $\text{rank}(P) = n - \text{nullity} = 5 - 1 = $ **4**.

pitfalls: Using the number of rows (4) in rank–nullity instead of the number of columns (5), which gives the wrong rank 3.

cse-2021-2-cs-26.approach: Property 1 means a prefix code, so the minimum is the Huffman cost. Among the tie choices, merge **a with d** (not b) so the later letter d gets the longer code — property 2 is then satisfied at the same optimal cost.

steps.title: Frequencies
steps.body: **abbccddeee**: a = 1, b = 2, c = 2, d = 2, e = 3 (total 10).

steps.title: Merge 1
steps.body: Smallest: a(1) and one of the 2s. To respect property 2, pair a with **d** (the latest of b, c, d): new node 3.

steps.title: Merge 2 and 3
steps.body: Remaining {b:2, c:2, ad:3, e:3}: merge b + c = 4, then ad(3) + e(3) = 6, then 4 + 6 = 10.

steps.title: Code lengths
steps.body:
b, c, e → 2 bits; a, d → 3 bits. Property 2: b (2) ≤ c (2) ≤ d (3) ✓.

Total $= 1\cdot3 + 2\cdot2 + 2\cdot2 + 2\cdot3 + 3\cdot2 = 3 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 = $ **23**.

optionAnalysis.reason: 21 is below the Huffman optimum (23) for these frequencies, so no prefix code achieves it.
Correct: Huffman cost 23 is achievable while respecting the tie rule.
25 is a valid but non-optimal assignment (e.g. lengths 2,2,3,3,3 with e longer).
30 is the fixed-length cost with 3-bit codes for all 10 letters.

pitfalls: Merging a with b gives the same cost but makes b (3 bits) longer than c, d (2 bits), violating property 2 — re-break the tie rather than changing the cost.
cse-2021-2-cs-26.verification: Kraft sum $3\cdot2^{-2} + 2\cdot2^{-3} = 1$, a full tree; any tie order of Huffman gives cost 23.

cse-2021-2-cs-27.approach: A write-through cache never holds dirty lines, so S1 holds. Write-allocate and write-through are independent choices (and the usual pairing is the reverse of S2), so S2 is false.

steps.title: Statement S1
steps.body: In write-through, every write updates L2 immediately, so L1 lines are always clean. Evicting a line on a read miss therefore needs **no writeback** → S1 **true**.

steps.title: Statement S2
steps.body: Allocation policy is independent of the write policy; no combination is mandatory. The common pairings are write-back + write-allocate and write-through + no-write-allocate — the opposite of S2. → S2 **false**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: write-through L1 has no dirty lines; S2’s “must” is false.
S1 is true, not false.
S2 is false — any write policy may be combined with either allocation policy.
S1 is true.

cse-2021-2-cs-27.verification: Dirty bits exist only in write-back caches; real write-through caches exist with both allocation policies.

cse-2021-2-cs-28.approach: An output 1 appears exactly when the current bit is 1 and the previous bit was 1. So the state only needs to remember the previous bit: $t = b$, and $y = s\,b$.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.body: A 1 is copied to the output unless it is the **first** 1 of a run, i.e. unless the previous bit was 0. Let state $s$ = previous input bit (initially 0).

steps.title: Next state
steps.body: After reading $b$, the previous bit becomes $b$: $t = b$.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: $y = 1$ iff $b = 1$ and previous bit $s = 1$: $y = s\,b$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $t = s + b$ never returns to state 0 after the first 1, so every later 1 (even the first of a new run) would be output.
Correct: state = previous bit, output = previous AND current.
$y = s\bar b$ outputs 1 on a 0 that follows a 1 — wrong.

cse-2021-2-cs-32.approach: Draw the precedence graph from conflicting pairs (P), then check whether any transaction reads a value written by an uncommitted transaction and commits first (Q).

steps.title: Conflicts on X
steps.body: $R_1(X), W_1(X)$ precede $R_3(X)$; the conflict is $W_1(X) \to R_3(X)$: edge $T_1 \to T_3$.

steps.title: Conflicts on Y
steps.body: $R_1(Y)$ before $W_2(Y)$: edge $T_1 \to T_2$ ($R_2(Y), W_2(Y)$ are the same transaction).

steps.title: Conflicts on Z
steps.body: $R_2(Z)$ before $W_3(Z)$: edge $T_2 \to T_3$ ($R_3(Z)$ vs $R_2(Z)$ is read–read, no conflict).

steps.title: P is true
steps.body: Edges $T_1\to T_2$, $T_1\to T_3$, $T_2\to T_3$ form no cycle → conflict-serializable, equivalent to $T_1, T_2, T_3$.

scene.caption: Acyclic → serial order T1, T2, T3

Correct: acyclic precedence graph; T3 reads X from T1.

cse-2021-2-cs-33.approach: Show by induction that in this (Pólya) urn the probability of red on every trial stays $\frac{r}{r+b}$: compute trial 2 explicitly and note the same algebra repeats.

steps.title: Trial 2
steps.body: $$P(R_2) = \frac{r}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r+1}{r+b+1} + \frac{b}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r}{r+b+1} = \frac{r(r+1+b)}{(r+b)(r+b+1)} = \frac{r}{r+b}$$

steps.title: Induction
steps.body: If before a trial the expected red fraction is $\frac{r}{r+b}$, then after it red count $R$ grows by 1 with probability $\frac{R}{N}$, so $E[\frac{R'}{N+1}] = E[\frac{R + R/N}{N+1}] = E[\frac{R}{N}]$. The red fraction is a martingale, so $P(R_k) = \frac{r}{r+b}$ for every $k$, in particular $k = 4$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $P(\text{red on 4th trial}) = \dfrac{r}{r+b}$ → **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: the probability of red is the same on every trial.
